title: Speaking up: when something at work doesn't feel right

audience.who: corporate employees across roles and levels
audience.knows: their day-to-day work and that a code of conduct exists, but not how to act on a doubt
audience.cares_about: doing the right thing without damaging their job or relationships

outcome: When something at work does not feel right, the viewer can pause, weigh what they noticed with a few honest questions, and raise it through the right channel without waiting for proof.
through_line: You do not need certainty to speak up: notice it, weigh it honestly, and take it to the right channel; raising a concern in good faith is protected.

arc_plan.what: Maya, an ordinary employee, notices something off at work (a record or expense that does not add up) and feels the familiar pull to say nothing.
By the end you will know what to do in that moment: how to weigh it and where to take it.
Why people stay quiet: fear of being wrong, of the fallout, or that it is not their business; Maya feels each one.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge sheet: reasons people stay silent

arc_plan.what: Weigh it: a few honest questions Maya asks herself; good faith means honest belief, not proof.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge sheet: good faith and weighing a concern

arc_plan.what: Use the right channel: her manager where comfortable, otherwise HR, compliance or a speak-up line, anonymous where offered; another route when the manager is involved.
What happens next: the concern is looked into and retaliation against a good-faith report is not allowed.
A short twist on Maya's story (the person involved is her own manager): which channel fits now?
Back to Maya: she raises it calmly through the right channel, and the uneasy opening moment is resolved.

must_cover.what: A good-faith concern does not require proof
The main speak-up channels, including an alternative when the manager is involved
Protection from retaliation for good-faith reports
Told as a short workplace story: one employee notices, weighs, and uses the right channel

must_avoid: made-up sayings attributed to real people
a specific real company's policy or hotline number
legal advice for a particular jurisdiction
opening with a glossary entry or agenda
example_posture: One ordinary office employee and an everyday, low-drama irregularity a colleague could plausibly notice; the same character carries the whole lesson. No villains, no dramatised wrongdoing.
visual_direction: A person in a situation: warm cartoon workplace scenes; the decision moment as a visible pause; the channels as a clear path the character can choose; the rule large where it matters; a before and after of her unease.
voice_note: A calm, warm colleague who has been there; respectful of the viewer's judgement, never lecturing; short plain sentences.
open_questions: Channel names vary by organisation; the lesson uses generic names (manager, HR, compliance, speak-up line).
